title: Where to Look Is Not How to Fix:Pre-Denoising Diagnostics and Modality-Dependent Controlin Diffusion Composition

paper.title: Where to Look Is Not How to Fix: Pre-Denoising Diagnostics and Modality-Dependent Control in Diffusion Composition
paper.abstract:
Abstract Understanding compositional failures in text-to-image diffusion
requires identifying both where stress is detectable and how
intervention changes the output. We study these questions
through a controlled anchor–stress protocol that jointly
evaluates text-encoder diagnostics and denoiser interventions.
We introduce a text-only Compositional Stress Index (CSI),
which separates common from rare compositions across SD1.5,
SDXL, and the SD3 text path and provides an upstream
diagnostic coordinate. A matched six-prompt localization
study links intervention location to distinct outcomes:
residual-minimizing embedding adapters improve
representation fit, while downstream cross-attention
intervention increases color hit rate (CHR) by 0.0272.
Across SD1.5 and SDXL denoiser blocks, the largest positive
signed diagnostic-accessibility mean occurs at the deep
encoder, whereas selective boost has its largest positive
mean CHR response at decoder blocks. Selective subtraction
and broad ablation reveal further modality- and
architecture-dependent responses, including a substantial
CHR decrease when SDXL decoder cross-attention is broadly
ablated.
We find a diagnosis-control dissociation under our
controlled attribute-object composition setting:
compositional defects are diagnosable before denoising,
but the representation coordinate that exposes risk is
not necessarily the coordinate or modality that improves
generation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image diffusion models [ 12 , 29 , 26 ] have achieved remarkable generation quality but remain brittle on semantically rare attribute–object compositions [ 14 , 36 ] : a model that reliably generates “a red car” may fail on “a blue pizza” or “a glass cat,” producing the wrong color, material, or texture. Two threads of work address this. Inference-time methods—Attend-and-Excite [ 4 ] , SynGen [ 28 ] , StructureDiffusion [ 8 ] , Divide-and-Bind [ 19 ] , and attention-map-controlled synthesis [ 35 ] —modify denoiser cross-attention so that attribute tokens better bind to the correct object regions, typically aggregating corrections across all layers. A second line of work studies the upstream text-conditioning pathway, asking whether compositional failures originate in representation geometry [ 17 , 3 ] or in misalignment between the embedding objective and the denoiser’s binding readout [ 37 , 22 ] . Implicit in both threads is an assumption: the pipeline location where a compositional defect is most detectable is also the location where it is most effectively correctable . We test this relationship by comparing diagnostic readouts and intervention responses at distinct pipeline sites. Our central finding is a site–modality dissociation: compositional stress has an upstream diagnostic signature, while intervention responses depend jointly on pipeline location and the type of edit. In the tested UNets, the deep encoder has the largest positive signed diagnostic-accessibility mean, whereas decoder blocks have the largest positive mean response to selective boost. This motivates treating diagnosis and intervention as distinct empirical questions: where to look is not how to fix . To make this concrete, consider modern text-to-image diffusion pipelines [ 29 , 27 , 30 , 26 , 7 ] . A text encoder first produces conditioning embeddings, which are then consumed by a denoising backbone to guide generation. In the UNet-based Stable Diffusion family, including SD1.5 and SDXL [ 29 , 26 ] , these conditioning embeddings are injected through cross-attention layers distributed across encoder, middle, and decoder blocks [ 29 , 11 , 33 ] . This architecture provides multiple internal sites at which a compositional failure may be readable, and multiple sites at which an intervention may affect the output. We use this UNet hierarchy for our block-level localization experiments, while also testing the representation-side diagnostic on an additional non-UNet text-to-image pipeline, namely Stable Diffusion 3 [ 7 ] . Our question is therefore: at which sites can compositional failures be detected , and at which can they be fixed —and does detection at a site imply fixability there? Table 1 maps this dissociation across three pipeline sites; rows correspond to sites, columns distinguish diagnostic readout from intervention outcomes. We present the evidence in two parts, corresponding to two regions of the pipeline. Upstream: diagnosis and repair at the text encoder (Table 1 , row 1). If a text encoder processes “a blue pizza” compositionally, the full-prompt representation should be roughly recoverable from the separate representations of “blue,” “pizza,” and the surrounding context. A large deviation from this component-based reconstruction indicates that the full prompt is not factorizing into its parts. We call this deviation a non-factorization residual and aggregate it into a Compositional Stress Index (CSI), where higher CSI indicates stronger departure from compositional factorization. Within a deliberately controlled anchor–stress setting that pairs common and rare attribute–object compositions while holding the object and context fixed, CSI separates the two groups perfectly (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, ROC-AUC = 1.0 {=}1.0 ) across SD1.5, SDXL, and the SD3 text path, and provides a diagnostic coordinate for the subsequent intervention analyses. We use the text-only CSI component for the pre-denoising interpretation (Appendix B ). This diagnostic coordinate lets us examine how representation changes relate to output changes. We train low-rank adapters to move stress embeddings toward anchor-like structure and compare their responses with denoiser-side cross-attention intervention. The adapters improve representation fit. On a matched six-prompt localization subset, downstream intervention increases CHR by 0.0272, while embedding intervention decreases it. The comparison connects intervention location to distinct representation and image-level outcomes under the tested objectives (§ 5 ). Downstream: per-block modality decomposition inside the denoiser (Table 1 , rows 2–3). This representation–output comparison motivates the downstream question: once text conditioning is read out by the denoiser, which internal sites are diagnostic, and which are causally controllable? For UNet-based SD1.5 and SDXL, we compare block groups spanning the deep encoder, middle block, and decoder, using three intervention modalities: selective boosting, selective zeroing, and broad cross-attention ablation. We quantify denoiser-side readout by diagnostic accessibility (DA), a block-level measure of how well cross-attention patterns separate anchor from stress prompts during baseline generation. The results reveal a second dissociation, now within the denoiser: D2 has the largest positive signed DA mean, while decoder blocks have the largest positive mean CHR response to selective boosting. Broad ablation produces a different, architecture-dependent profile, with a substantial CHR decrease at SDXL U0 and at early SD1.5 encoder blocks. These profiles characterize how intervention responses vary with both where an edit is applied and how it modifies cross-attention (§ 6 ).

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: (1) Under the tested intervention families, we uncover a diagnosis–control dissociation in text-to-image diffusion: the site where compositional stress is most readable is not necessarily the site where intervention is most effective. (2) We further decompose this dissociation under the tested intervention families, showing that selective token edits and broad cross-attention ablations have different site profiles across deep encoder and decoder blocks. (3) We introduce text-only CSI as a pre-denoising stress coordinate and evaluate it across SD1.5, SDXL, and the SD3 text path under the controlled anchor–stress protocol. (4) Under the tested intervention families, we connect representation and output responses through a matched localization study: residual-minimizing adapters improve embedding fit, while downstream intervention increases CHR on the selected six-prompt subset. sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: The cross-attention-steering methods introduced in § 1 [ 4 , 28 , 8 , 19 , 35 ] share a design choice: they aggregate attention signal across all layers and resolutions, treating cross-attention as a homogeneous control surface; logit-level masking and entity-region constraints (e.g., MaskDiffusion-style methods, box-guided attention control) target specific resolutions or layers but similarly do not decompose across stages. WiCLP [ 37 ] pivots upstream, showing embedding-level repair can work with supervision aligned to the denoiser’s readout and implicating objective misalignment rather than the embedding space itself. Our findings should not be interpreted as evidence that all upstream interventions fail. WiCLP, for instance, demonstrates that embedding-space interventions can improve compositional generation when optimized with denoising-aligned objectives. Our result is narrower: reducing the CSI-diagnosed residual via residual minimization is not sufficient to guarantee semantic improvement. Marioriyad et al. [22] link entity-missing to attention overlap. A complementary line of work intervenes at training or sampling time rather than at inference attention, including contrastive curriculum fine-tuning [ 10 ] , sampling-time corrective steering [ 6 ] , and PAC-Bayesian priors over attention distributions [ 15 ] . Our contribution is orthogonal to all of these: we diagnose where in the pipeline compositional risk appears and characterize which modality works at each site, producing a layer-selection principle that could inform any of these approaches—training-time methods might focus supervision on the deep-encoder representation we identify, while sampling-time correctors gain most by operating on decoder-side attention. On the representation and evaluation side, CLIP embeddings admit sparse linear decompositions [ 3 ] and compose single-object attributes but fail under multi-object binding [ 17 ] . Prompt-to-Prompt [ 11 ] showed cross-attention encodes spatial and semantic structure; FreeU [ 31 ] demonstrated that UNet encoder–decoder information flow is a control axis. More broadly, probing and causal intervention research [ 1 , 2 , 34 , 9 , 24 ] has shown that probe-friendly layers need not be intervention-friendly. We sharpen this gap for diffusion cross-attention by identifying both which layer and which modality works at each layer, and we quantify a pre-denoising non-factorization signal not captured by these prior analyses. Output-side benchmarks [ 14 , 32 , 18 ] measure whether composition fails; our work diagnoses where the failure originates and how to intervene at each site. Extended related work covering compositional evaluation suites, object-centric representations, and energy-based compositional generation appears in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 3 Setup: Sites, Diagnostics, and Interventions
sections.text: We study controlled compositional stress in text-to-image diffusion. Each example consists of an anchor prompt paired with a single stress prompt that shares the same object and context but differs in the target attribute. The anchor uses a common attribute–object composition, whereas the stress prompt uses a rarer or less typical composition. Given such pairs, we ask two questions: where in the model is the stress signal diagnostically readable, and where can an intervention causally improve the generated output? Our experiments instantiate this setup with 432 prompts organized into 216 paired groups, each consisting of one anchor prompt and one stress prompt. Attribute–object combinations are selected from T2I-CompBench [ 14 ] , CLEVR [ 16 ] , and ARO [ 36 ] lexicons to span common and rare compositional regimes (examples in Appendix N ). For example, within one group the anchor might be “a studio photo of a red pizza” and the stress prompt “a studio photo of a blue pizza”—same object, same context, different attribute. Examples such as “a red car” and “a blue pizza” that appear elsewhere in the paper illustrate the rarity gradient across the dataset, not within-pair variation. Primary models for generation and denoiser-side intervention are SD1.5 and SDXL, while SD3 is used only for text-path diagnostic extension. For UNet block-group analysis, we partition cross-attention modules by their position in the UNet architecture. Following standard notation, D k D_{k} denotes the k k -th down-sampling (encoder) stage, M M the middle bottleneck, and U k U_{k} the k k -th up-sampling (decoder) stage. SDXL has five active cross-attention groups: { D 1 , D 2 , M , U 0 , U 1 } \{D_{1},D_{2},M,U_{0},U_{1}\} ; SD1.5 has seven: { D 0 , D 1 , D 2 , M , U 1 , U 2 , U 3 } \{D_{0},D_{1},D_{2},M,U_{1},U_{2},U_{3}\} (module counts per group in Appendix K ). Throughout, we refer to D 2 D_{2} as the deep encoder and U 0 U_{0} (SDXL) / U 1 U_{1} (SD1.5) as the decoder . With these sites defined, we next introduce two diagnostic readouts—one at the text encoder, one inside the denoiser—and two families of intervention: embedding-level repair and denoiser-side cross-attention edits.

sections.heading: Text-encoder diagnostic: CSI.
sections.text: We operationalize text-side compositionality as a component-reconstruction test. If the text encoder preserves a factorized representation of attribute, object, and context, then a simple composition rule should explain the full-prompt embedding; large residuals indicate prompt-specific interactions beyond this factorized account. For each prompt p full p_{\mathrm{full}} (e.g., “a studio photo of a blue pizza”), we construct component inputs: p attr p_{\mathrm{attr}} (the target attribute, e.g., “blue”), p obj p_{\mathrm{obj}} (the object, e.g., “pizza”), and p ctx p_{\mathrm{ctx}} (the surrounding context template). Let h ⁡ ( ⋅ ) h(\cdot) denote the representation extracted from the text encoder, and let h ^ ​ ( ⋅ ) \hat{h}(\cdot) be a deliberately low-capacity composition model fit to predict h ⁡ ( p full ) h(p_{\mathrm{full}}) from the component representations. We consider additive, low-rank linear, and low-rank bilinear variants, fit on anchor prompts and evaluated on both anchor and stress prompts. We define the non-factorization residual as R ⁡ ( p full ) = ‖ h ⁡ ( p full ) − h ^ ​ ( p attr , p obj , p ctx ) ‖ 2 ‖ h ⁡ ( p full ) ‖ 2 + ε . R(p_{\mathrm{full}})=\frac{\left\lVert h(p_{\mathrm{full}})-\hat{h}(p_{\mathrm{attr}},p_{\mathrm{obj}},p_{\mathrm{ctx}})\right\rVert_{2}}{\left\lVert h(p_{\mathrm{full}})\right\rVert_{2}+\varepsilon}. (1) where ε \varepsilon prevents division by zero. In plain terms: If the encoder preserves component-wise structure for “blue,” “pizza,” and the context template, then a simple composition model should be able to reconstruct the full-prompt embedding, yielding a small R R . If the full prompt instead induces prompt-specific interactions that are not predictable from those components, the residual increases. CSI aggregates this normalized residual with span-geometry features via robust standardization on anchor statistics; we report CSI text \mathrm{CSI}_{\mathrm{text}} , CSI span \mathrm{CSI}_{\mathrm{span}} , and combined CSI \mathrm{CSI} . Only CSI text \mathrm{CSI}_{\mathrm{text}} is strictly pre-denoising; combined CSI includes internal attention-derived span features. Encoder extraction, calibration scope, and span-feature definitions are given in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Denoiser diagnostic: DA.
sections.text: The second diagnostic readout operates inside the denoiser. For each UNet block group b b , diagnostic accessibility DA ⁡ ( b ) \mathrm{DA}(b) measures how well block-level cross-attention patterns distinguish anchor from stress prompts during baseline generation. We define an attribute-binding measure ABM b \mathrm{ABM}_{b} as the fraction of attribute-token attention mass falling within top-quantile object-attention regions, then compute: DA ⁡ ( b ) = 𝔼 ( p a , p s ) ​ [ ABM b ​ ( p a ) − ABM b ​ ( p s ) ] , \mathrm{DA}(b)=\mathbb{E}_{(p_{a},\,p_{s})}\bigl[\mathrm{ABM}_{b}(p_{a})-\mathrm{ABM}_{b}(p_{s})\bigr], (2) where ( p a , p s ) (p_{a},p_{s}) denotes a matched anchor–stress pair. Positive DA means anchor prompts show tighter attribute-to-object binding at block b b than stress prompts. We rank sites by this signed mean difference; negative DA indicates the reverse contrast and is not evidence of absent diagnostic information. Significance against zero does not establish a significant difference between sites. Formal definitions and validation of ABM are given in Appendix H . To separate where an intervention is applied from what kind of intervention it is, we organize denoiser-side edits along two axes: selectivity , whether the edit targets only the attribute token or the entire cross-attention map, and sign , whether the edit strengthens or weakens the conditioning channel. This gives a 2 × 2 2{\times}2 design; the broad-additive cell is omitted because uniformly scaling all attention weights is canceled by post-softmax normalization, leaving three testable denoiser-side families. Selective additive ( boost ) amplifies attention to the target attribute token at a chosen block, testing whether stronger local attribute readout improves binding. Selective subtractive ( attr_zero ) removes the same attribute-token attention, testing the opposite direction as a matched-selectivity control. Broad subtractive ( zero ) uniformly flattens all cross-attention at a chosen block, testing whether the block’s entire text-conditioning contribution is necessary or harmful. Together with two embedding-level repair families—pooled and token low-rank adapters trained to move stress representations toward anchor-like structure—this yields five intervention families. Implementation details and statistical testing protocols are given in Appendix D . These three denoiser modalities span a natural hypothesis space about the defect’s structure. If the failure reflects weak attribute readout, boost should help by amplifying the target-attribute channel. If the same channel is causally involved but harmful or mislocalized, attr_zero tests the opposite direction by removing it. If the failure is distributed across the block’s entire text-conditioning pathway, zero tests whether removing that contribution improves generation. Testing all three at each block allows us to diagnose not just where the defect is, but what kind of defect it is. All intervention hyperparameters are fixed across block comparisons (strength, mask quantile, timestep schedule, and CFG settings in Appendix D ). We evaluate control with object-local color hit rate (CHR): the fraction of pixels inside a fixed target-object mask whose color matches the desired attribute. The object mask is derived from baseline final-timestep attention and held fixed across conditions, which fixes the scoring region but does not independently verify object identity or localization; mask stability across interventions is verified in Appendix I . In the full per-block runs, CHR is finite for 52 stress prompts per seed; the other 164 stress prompts have no target color recorded by the scorer. This is a scoring-eligibility criterion, not a verified taxonomy of prompt semantics. We use chromatic binding because it changes attribute semantics while largely preserving object shape and localization, providing the cleanest endpoint for site-localization comparisons. Color prototypes and thresholds are reported in Appendix I . For the audited per-block results, we first average paired differences across seeds, then test across prompts (CE) or matched group_id units (DA). We use two-sided sign-flip tests (5,000 Monte Carlo draws, plus-one correction; exact enumeration for at most 16 units) and 2,000 percentile-bootstrap draws, with analysis seed 0. BH correction is applied separately to DA and CE across all active blocks within each model/run. Full CE analyses use 52 prompts with five seeds for boost/attr-zero and three for broad zeroing; DA uses 216 groups. Group IDs do not by themselves establish independence of shared anchor texts.

sections.heading: 4 Result 1: Text Encoders Provide a Pre-Denoising Stress Axis
sections.text: We first ask whether compositional stress is already visible before denoising, using only text-encoder representations. The goal is not to establish CSI as a general-purpose detector of arbitrary compositional failure, but to obtain a calibrated axis that orders prompts by stress severity before testing where intervention can change the generated output. On the controlled anchor–stress protocol, CSI cleanly separates common-composition anchors from rare-composition stress prompts across SD1.5, SDXL, and the SD3 text path (ROC-AUC = 1.0 {=}1.0 , pair-ranking = 1.0 {=}1.0 ; Figure 2 ). This ceiling-level separation should be interpreted with the protocol in mind: stress prompts are deliberately constructed to be semantically rare, and a frequency-only baseline already reaches ROC-AUC = 0.79 {=}0.79 . Thus, the important claim is not that CSI is a universal binary detector, but that text-side non-factorization provides a stable pre-denoising stress coordinate. Figure 1 : Prompt-level CSI distributions for anchor and stress prompts across SD1.5, SDXL, and SD3. Values are displayed on a MAD-normalized symlog scale. Although absolute magnitudes are not directly comparable across models, stress prompts consistently occupy a much higher CSI regime than anchor prompts. This visualization complements ROC-AUC by showing the magnitude of the anchor–stress separation. While ROC-AUC summarizes ranking performance, Figure 1 visualizes the underlying prompt-level distributions. Across all three models, stress prompts exhibit substantially larger CSI values than anchors, consistent with the near-perfect separation reported above. The stronger evidence is that CSI remains informative within the stress set and aligns with output-side failures. Across stress prompts, CSI correlates with graded stress severity (decile-stress Spearman ρ = 0.87 \rho{=}0.87 ) and with BLIP-derived attribute failure rate (Spearman ρ = 0.68 \rho{=}0.68 ); output-side BLIP-VQA labels ( n = 4320 n{=}4320 ) show that CSI predicts attribute failure with ROC-AUC = 0.89 {=}0.89 and binding failure with ROC-AUC = 0.85 {=}0.85 . Controls support this interpretation: group-preserving permutation gives null ROC-AUC = 0.49 ± 0.01 =0.49\pm 0.01 (all empirical p = 0.001 p{=}0.001 ), text-side non-factorization is the dominant contributor, span-only geometry is substantially weaker, and robustness to lexical confounds and family ablations is reported in Appendix B . The pattern is also consistent across encoder families: SD1.5 uses a single CLIP text encoder, SDXL uses dual encoders (CLIP-L + OpenCLIP-G), and the SD3 text-path extension uses a T5-XXL sequence mean. Despite these architectural differences, the non-factorization gap appears in all three settings, so we use CSI as a model-agnostic pre-denoising stratification axis for the intervention analyses in § 5 –§ 6 . Figure 2 : Cross-model CSI decile curves. Probability of stress membership increases monotonically with CSI decile; SD1.5, SDXL, and SD3 collapse to the same transition pattern. ROC-AUC = 1.0 {=}1.0 in all three models.

sections.heading: 5 Result 2: Upstream Representation Repair Does Not Imply Semantic Repair
sections.text: The upstream analysis established that compositional stress is detectable at the text encoder. We next ask whether repairing that diagnostic coordinate is sufficient to improve generated output. A pooled adapter reduces the representation residual ( Δ repr = − 0.100 \Delta_{\text{repr}}{=}-0.100 , q = 0.0024 q{=}0.0024 , 20 prompts), and a token adapter gives Δ repr = − 0.184 \Delta_{\text{repr}}{=}-0.184 ( q = 0.0008 q{=}0.0008 , 19 prompts). Each has seven CHR-evaluable prompts, with observed Δ CHR = 0 \Delta_{\text{CHR}}{=}0 ( q = 1 q{=}1 ). On a separate CSI-stratified localization subset with six CHR-evaluable prompts and five seeds each, downstream intervention increases CHR by + 0.0272 +0.0272 (95% CI [ 0.0092 , 0.0469 ] [0.0092,0.0469] ; exact prompt-level p = 0.03125 p{=}0.03125 , q = 0.046875 q{=}0.046875 , d z = 1.04 d_{z}{=}1.04 ), whereas token-level embedding repair decreases CHR by − 0.0680 -0.0680 (95% CI [ − 0.1071 , − 0.0327 ] [-0.1071,-0.0327] ; p = 0.03125 p{=}0.03125 , q = 0.03125 q{=}0.03125 ). The two arms use the same six prompts and seeds and have identical baseline CHR values. These results concern the measured CHR endpoint and do not establish general semantic repair. A separate rank sweep (4–128) shows no significant positive CHR effect for the pooled adapters and negative CHR effects for the token adapters under within-run correction (Appendix C ). Residual improvement is not monotonic in rank, and these data do not rule out capacity or objective choice as explanations. In the localization downstream arm, early ABM increases ( Δ = 0.000450 \Delta{=}0.000450 , q = 0.0012 q{=}0.0012 ), whereas the mid-ABM change does not reach significance ( Δ = 0.000257 \Delta{=}0.000257 , q = 0.0708 q{=}0.0708 ). This pattern motivates, but does not identify, distinct readout mechanisms. We interpret this as a representation–generation boundary: the upstream coordinate that diagnoses compositional stress is not automatically a control coordinate for the denoiser’s binding behavior. This conclusion is specific to residual-minimizing objectives; it does not rule out embedding-level repair with binding-aligned supervision such as WiCLP [ 37 ] . The next question is whether the binding channel can be reached more directly inside the denoiser, and if so, at which blocks and with which modality. § 6 addresses this with a per-block sweep of cross-attention interventions.

sections.heading: 7 Discussion
sections.text: Taken together, the upstream and downstream analyses reveal a specific property of diffusion pipelines: as the conditioning representation flows from text encoder to denoiser cross-attention, the features that are most informative about which prompts will fail and the features that are most responsive to interventions that correct failure live in different places. Text-encoder residuals provide a diagnostic coordinate; D2 has the largest positive signed DA mean; and decoder blocks have the largest positive boost CE means. Together these measurements locate distinct diagnostic and intervention-response profiles along the pipeline. The site-level mismatch extends to the prompt level as well: CSI-stratified analysis shows no consistent positive correlation between pre-denoising stress severity and decoder boost response (SDXL partial ρ = − 0.17 \rho{=}-0.17 , p = 0.007 p{=}0.007 ; SD1.5 ρ = + 0.11 \rho{=}+0.11 , ns), so diagnostic severity does not predict which prompts respond to intervention. Diagnosis and intervention are not aligned by default along the pipeline; whether they can be realigned depends on choices about objective (embedding repair, § 5 ) and modality (per-block decomposition, § 6 ), not merely site. Two mechanistic observations sharpen the dissociation. At D2, neither tested token-level intervention shows an FDR-significant CHR effect and per-timestep analysis shows DA–CE anti-correlation—D2 is most diagnostic in early denoising precisely when boost is most destructive. We interpret this carefully: our tested attribute-token operators (additive boost, matched-selectivity zeroing, fractional attenuation) do not reach the defect, but the underlying structure is not uniquely identified, since the pattern is equally consistent with a distributed defect across D2’s cross-attention output and with a localized defect in a representation subspace our operators miss. At the decoder, U0’s negative DA ( − 0.0118 -0.0118 , FDR q = 0.00033 q{=}0.00033 in the SDXL boost baseline) indicates a reverse anchor–stress ABM contrast; the decoder does not lack signal but faithfully executes whatever binding it receives, including incorrect upstream binding. Overriding existing binding with a competing signal is one possible interpretation, not a mechanism established by these comparisons. These findings motivate evaluating diagnostic readouts and intervention operators jointly while selecting intervention sites using measured output responses. Beyond our own protocol, the modality–site dissociation has implications for existing inference-time methods. Attend-and-Excite [ 4 ] and SynGen [ 28 ] apply gradient-based corrections across all cross-attention layers simultaneously; our per-block decomposition suggests their effectiveness may concentrate at decoder blocks, because decoder blocks have the largest positive boost CE means in our sweeps. If the encoder-side contribution is zero or negative, all-layer methods may succeed despite their encoder-side component rather than because of it—a testable prediction: restricting A&E/SynGen updates to decoder-only cross-attention should preserve or improve performance while reducing compute, and restricting to encoder-only should degrade performance to baseline or worse. More broadly, the diagnosis–control mismatch is not specific to diffusion models. Any system with a separated encoder and decoder—including encoder-decoder language models, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, and vision-language models—faces the same structural question: does diagnosing a defect in the encoder tell you how to fix it in the decoder? Our results suggest the answer is not automatic. The features that make a defect visible (high mutual information with the anchor/stress label) need not be the features that make it fixable (responsive to targeted intervention). Intervention design must be informed by the decoder’s readout structure, not merely by the encoder’s diagnostic signal.

sections.heading: 7.1 Scope and Interpretation
sections.text: The central conclusion of this work is not that a particular intervention site universally solves compositional failures. Rather, our evidence establishes that diagnostic accessibility, representation modification, and semantic improvement should not be assumed to coincide. Accordingly, we do not claim (i) that all upstream interventions fail, (ii) that decoder-side intervention provides a universal repair mechanism, or (iii) that the observed diagnosis-control dissociation has been established for relational or role-binding compositions. Our results are supported for the evaluated attribute-object setting and the tested intervention modalities.

sections.heading: 8 Limitations
sections.text: We distinguish established from suggestive findings. Established : (i) CSI separates anchor from stress cross-model (ROC-AUC = 1.0 {=}1.0 , permutation null = 0.49 {=}0.49 , within-stress ρ = 0.68 \rho{=}0.68 ), though partly reflecting the controlled protocol; (ii) D2 has the largest positive signed DA mean in the six baseline datasets and differs from zero after FDR; these are not six independent replications; (iii) selective subtraction shows no significant positive CHR effect across the reported blocks; (iv) embedding repair reduces residuals without semantic improvement. Suggestive : (v) decoder boost as a preferred selective site (baseline contrasts nominally significant in both models but not after per-block FDR; decoder-minus-D2 significant only in SDXL); (vi) D2 defect structure (consistent with but not uniquely identified by our operators); (vii) generality beyond chromatic binding. Key caveats: boost CE is small ( + 0.006 +0.006 – 0.008 0.008 ) and does not survive within-model FDR; CE is color-only (52 valid prompts per seed); SD3 is text-path only; two UNet architectures, no DiT; fixed intervention hyperparameters; CSI-based routing and a universal decoder repair interface unvalidated; broad-additive cell untested; WiCLP-aligned embedding repair not tested; object mask from baseline attention, held fixed across conditions (empirically verified stable: median | Δ | = 0.2 % |\Delta|{=}0.2\% , p ​ 95 = 1.5 % p95{=}1.5\% , r ≥ 0.92 r{\geq}0.92 ). We characterize a modality-dependent structure, not a universal law. External-mask and background-color sensitivity checks further limit the interpretation to a small chromatic response rather than established object-local semantic repair (Appendix J ).

sections.heading: 9 Conclusion
sections.text: We characterize compositional diagnosis and intervention through complementary measurements of text representations, cross-attention, and generated color agreement. Text-only CSI provides an upstream stress coordinate across SD1.5, SDXL, and the SD3 text path under the controlled anchor–stress protocol. Within the two tested UNets, the largest positive signed DA mean occurs at D2, while the largest positive selective-boost CE mean occurs at decoder blocks. A matched six-prompt localization study further links intervention location to output response, with downstream intervention increasing CHR as residual-minimizing adapters improve representation fit. Broad ablation reveals distinct architecture-dependent sensitivity profiles. Together, these findings provide an empirical site–modality map and motivate choosing intervention sites through output-response evaluation alongside diagnostic analysis. Extending this framework to broader compositional benchmarks, binding-aligned objectives, and DiT backbones offers concrete directions for future work. Code, CSI computation scripts, prompts, and seeds will be released on GitHub upon publication.

sections.heading: Appendix A Extended Related Work
sections.text: A growing body of work examines compositional generation and evaluation in controlled settings. Okawa et al. [25] show that compositional abilities in diffusion models emerge multiplicatively rather than additively, consistent with our finding that compositional entanglement in text representations resists simple additive decomposition. Marioriyad et al. [23] provide a systematic evaluation comparing diffusion and autoregressive architectures on compositionality, reinforcing that compositional failures are architecture-general. Broader evaluation suites—T2I-CompBench++ [ 14 ] , Winoground [ 32 ] , CREPE [ 21 ] , and SugarCrepe [ 13 ] —measure compositional success at the output level across attribute, relation, and object categories; our work is complementary, diagnosing where inside the pipeline these failures originate rather than whether they occur. Object-centric and disentangled representation learning [ 20 ] provides a conceptual parallel: slot-based models enforce compositional structure by design, whereas text-to-image diffusion models inherit whatever compositional structure CLIP-family encoders provide. Energy-based compositional generation [ 5 ] offers an alternative compositional mechanism through explicit concept combination at sampling time. Our per-block analysis connects to these perspectives by showing that D2’s cross-attention—the site where compositional defects are most visible—does not support token-level decomposition of the defect, consistent with a representation that lacks the disentangled structure needed for targeted repair.

sections.heading: Calibration and diagnostic scope.
sections.text: The saved discovery scores use all anchors within each model for this standardization, separately from fold-wise composition fitting. They therefore do not establish fully held-out calibration or deployment performance. Pair-level partitions can also share an anchor text across groups and do not establish generalization to unseen anchor texts. The saved span features include internal mid-attention quantities, so only CSI text \mathrm{CSI}_{\mathrm{text}} supports a strictly pre-denoising interpretation; combined-CSI associations are retrospective diagnostics and should not be attributed to a text-only score without recomputation. Discovery is assessed by a Ladder Consistency Criterion (LCC): monotonic decile trend, first-to-last delta CI excluding 0, and consistent direction across models. The stricter Correlation Threshold Sensitivity check ( ρ ≥ 0.90 \rho\geq 0.90 ) is reported as sensitivity analysis only. Several robustness analyses confirm that the CSI signal is not an artifact. Group-preserving label-permutation yields null ROC-AUC = 0.49 ± 0.01 =0.49\pm 0.01 against a true ROC-AUC of 0.89 0.89 – 1.00 1.00 (all empirical p = 0.001 p=0.001 ), and CSI ROC-AUC = 1.0 {=}1.0 holds in all four conflict-type strata (chromatic oddness, material–object, geometric pattern, state–environment), so the signal is not driven by a single attribute class. We further apply a three-level covariate control protocol. Level 1 uses covariate-adjusted analyses controlling for perplexity, subtoken count, attribute frequency, prompt length, and template family. Level 2 uses near-matched subsets ( n pairs = 140 n_{\text{pairs}}{=}140 , canonical tier); near-matched LOGO residual effects remain significant (linear mean diff = 0.543 {=}0.543 , q < 0.001 q{<}0.001 ; bilinear mean diff = 0.681 {=}0.681 , q < 0.001 q{<}0.001 ), and strict ( n = 112 n{=}112 ) and relaxed ( n = 178 n{=}178 ) tiers preserve the same pattern. A predictive-asymmetry breakdown clarifies which CSI families carry the signal. WiCLP [ 37 ] uses a binding-aligned objective, so our findings remain specific to the tested residual-minimizing objectives. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.03068v1 [cs.CV] 02 Oct 2026 Where to Look Is Not How to Fix: Pre-Denoising Diagnostics and Modality-Dependent Control in Diffusion Composition Fangzheng Wu Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: Tulane University Affiliation: New Orleans, LA 70118 Email: fwu6@tulane.edu Brian Summa Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: Tulane University Affiliation: New Orleans, LA 70118 Email: bsumma@tulane.edu Abstract Understanding compositional failures in text-to-image diffusion requires identifying both where stress is detectable and how intervention changes the output. We study these questions through a controlled anchor–stress protocol that jointly evaluates text-encoder diagnostics and denoiser interventions. We introduce a text-only Compositional Stress Index (CSI), which separates common from rare compositions across SD1.5, SDXL, and the SD3 text path and provides an upstream diagnostic coordinate. A matched six-prompt localization study links intervention location to distinct outcomes: residual-minimizing embedding adapters improve representation fit, while downstream cross-attention intervention increases color hit rate (CHR) by 0.0272. Across SD1.5 and SDXL denoiser blocks, the largest positive signed diagnostic-accessibility mean occurs at the deep encoder, whereas selective boost has its largest positive mean CHR response at decoder blocks. Selective subtraction and broad ablation reveal further modality- and architecture-dependent responses, including a substantial CHR decrease when SDXL decoder cross-attention is broadly ablated. We find a diagnosis-control dissociation under our controlled attribute-object composition setting: compositional defects are diagnosable before denoising, but the representation coordinate that exposes risk is not necessarily the coordinate or modality that improves generation. 1 Introduction Text-to-image diffusion models [ 12 , 29 , 26 ] have achieved remarkable generation quality but remain brittle on semantically rare attribute–object compositions [ 14 , 36 ] : a model that reliably generates “a red car” may fail on “a blue pizza” or “a glass cat,” producing the wrong color, material, or texture. Two threads of work address this. Inference-time methods—Attend-and-Excite [ 4 ] , SynGen [ 28 ] , StructureDiffusion [ 8 ] , Divide-and-Bind [ 19 ] , and attention-map-controlled synthesis [ 35 ] —modify denoiser cross-attention so that attribute tokens better bind to the correct object regions, typically aggregating corrections across all layers. A second line of work studies the upstream text-conditioning pathway, asking whether compositional failures originate in representation geometry [ 17 , 3 ] or in misalignment between the embedding objective and the denoiser’s binding readout [ 37 , 22 ] . Implicit in both threads is an assumption: the pipeline location where a compositional defect is most detectable is also the location where it is most effectively correctable . We test this relationship by comparing diagnostic readouts and intervention responses at distinct pipeline sites. Our central finding is a site–modality dissociation: compositional stress has an upstream diagnostic signature, while intervention responses depend jointly on pipeline location and the type of edit. In the tested UNets, the deep encoder has the largest positive signed diagnostic-accessibility mean, whereas decoder blocks have the largest positive mean response to selective boost. This motivates treating diagnosis and intervention as distinct empirical questions: where to look is not how to fix . To make this concrete, consider modern text-to-image diffusion pipelines [ 29 , 27 , 30 , 26 , 7 ] . A text encoder first produces conditioning embeddings, which are then consumed by a denoising backbone to guide generation. In the UNet-based Stable Diffusion family, including SD1.5 and SDXL [ 29 , 26 ] , these conditioning embeddings are injected through cross-attention layers distributed across encoder, middle, and decoder blocks [ 29 , 11 , 33 ] . This architecture provides multiple internal sites at which a compositional failure may be readable, and multiple sites at which an intervention may affect the output. We use this UNet hierarchy for our block-level localization experiments, while also testing the representation-side diagnostic on an additional non-UNet text-to-image pipeline, namely Stable Diffusion 3 [ 7 ] . Our question is therefore: at which sites can compositional failures be detected , and at which can they be fixed —and does detection at a site imply fixability there? Table 1 maps this dissociation across three pipeline sites; rows correspond to sites, columns distinguish diagnostic readout from intervention outcomes. We present the evidence in two parts, corresponding to two regions of the pipeline. Upstream: diagnosis and repair at the text encoder (Table 1 , row 1). If a text encoder processes “a blue pizza” compositionally, the full-prompt representation should be roughly recoverable from the separate representations of “blue,” “pizza,” and the surrounding context. A large deviation from this component-based reconstruction indicates that the full prompt is not factorizing into its parts. We call this deviation a non-factorization residual and aggregate it into a Compositional Stress Index (CSI), where higher CSI indicates stronger departure from compositional factorization. Within a deliberately controlled anchor–stress setting that pairs common and rare attribute–object compositions while holding the object and context fixed, CSI separates the two groups perfectly (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, ROC-AUC = 1.0 {=}1.0 ) across SD1.5, SDXL, and the SD3 text path, and provides a diagnostic coordinate for the subsequent intervention analyses. We use the text-only CSI component for the pre-denoising interpretation (Appendix B ). This diagnostic coordinate lets us examine how representation changes relate to output changes. We train low-rank adapters to move stress embeddings toward anchor-like structure and compare their responses with denoiser-side cross-attention intervention. The adapters improve representation fit. On a matched six-prompt localization subset, downstream intervention increases CHR by 0.0272, while embedding intervention decreases it. The comparison connects intervention location to distinct representation and image-level outcomes under the tested objectives (§ 5 ). Downstream: per-block modality decomposition inside the denoiser (Table 1 , rows 2–3). This representation–output comparison motivates the downstream question: once text conditioning is read out by the denoiser, which internal sites are diagnostic, and which are causally controllable? For UNet-based SD1.5 and SDXL, we compare block groups spanning the deep encoder, middle block, and decoder, using three intervention modalities: selective boosting, selective zeroing, and broad cross-attention ablation. We quantify denoiser-side readout by diagnostic accessibility (DA), a block-level measure of how well cross-attention patterns separate anchor from stress prompts during baseline generation. The results reveal a second dissociation, now within the denoiser: D2 has the largest positive signed DA mean, while decoder blocks have the largest positive mean CHR response to selective boosting. Broad ablation produces a different, architecture-dependent profile, with a substantial CHR decrease at SDXL U0 and at early SD1.5 encoder blocks. These profiles characterize how intervention responses vary with both where an edit is applied and how it modifies cross-attention (§ 6 ). Contributions. (1) Under the tested intervention families, we uncover a diagnosis–control dissociation in text-to-image diffusion: the site where compositional stress is most readable is not necessarily the site where intervention is most effective. (2) We further decompose this dissociation under the tested intervention families, showing that selective token edits and broad cross-attention ablations have different site profiles across deep encoder and decoder blocks. (3) We introduce text-only CSI as a pre-denoising stress coordinate and evaluate it across SD1.5, SDXL, and the SD3 text path under the controlled anchor–stress protocol. (4) Under the tested intervention families, we connect representation and output responses through a matched localization study: residual-minimizing adapters improve embedding fit, while downstream intervention increases CHR on the selected six-prompt subset. WiCLP [ 37 ] pivots upstream, showing embedding-level repair can work with supervision aligned to the denoiser’s readout and implicating objective misalignment rather than the embedding space itself. Our findings should not be interpreted as evidence that all upstream interventions fail. WiCLP, for instance, demonstrates that embedding-space interventions can improve compositional generation when optimized with denoising-aligned objectives. Our result is narrower: reducing the CSI-diagnosed residual via residual minimization is not sufficient to guarantee semantic improvement. Marioriyad et al. [22] link entity-missing to attention overlap. A complementary line of work intervenes at training or sampling time rather than at inference attention, including contrastive curriculum fine-tuning [ 10 ] , sampling-time corrective steering [ 6 ] , and PAC-Bayesian priors over attention distributions [ 15 ] . Our contribution is orthogonal to all of these: we diagnose where in the pipeline compositional risk appears and characterize which modality works at each site, producing a layer-selection principle that could inform any of these approaches—training-time methods might focus supervision on the deep-encoder representation we identify, while sampling-time correctors gain most by operating on decoder-side attention. On the representation and evaluation side, CLIP embeddings admit sparse linear decompositions [ 3 ] and compose single-object attributes but fail under multi-object binding [ 17 ] . Prompt-to-Prompt [ 11 ] showed cross-attention encodes spatial and semantic structure; FreeU [ 31 ] demonstrated that UNet encoder–decoder information flow is a control axis. More broadly, probing and causal intervention research [ 1 , 2 , 34 , 9 , 24 ] has shown that probe-friendly layers need not be intervention-friendly. We sharpen this gap for diffusion cross-attention by identifying both which layer and which modality works at each layer, and we quantify a pre-denoising non-factorization signal not captured by these prior analyses. Output-side benchmarks [ 14 , 32 , 18 ] measure whether composition fails; our work diagnoses where the failure originates and how to intervene at each site. Extended related work covering compositional evaluation suites, object-centric representations, and energy-based compositional generation appears in Appendix A . 3 Setup: Sites, Diagnostics, and Interventions We study controlled compositional stress in text-to-image diffusion. Each example consists of an anchor prompt paired with a single stress prompt that shares the same object and context but differs in the target attribute. The anchor uses a common attribute–object composition, whereas the stress prompt uses a rarer or less typical composition. Given such pairs, we ask two questions: where in the model is the stress signal diagnostically readable, and where can an intervention causally improve the generated output? Our experiments instantiate this setup with 432 prompts organized into 216 paired groups, each consisting of one anchor prompt and one stress prompt. Attribute–object combinations are selected from T2I-CompBench [ 14 ] , CLEVR [ 16 ] , and ARO [ 36 ] lexicons to span common and rare compositional regimes (examples in Appendix N ). For example, within one group the anchor might be “a studio photo of a red pizza” and the stress prompt “a studio photo of a blue pizza”—same object, same context, different attribute. Examples such as “a red car” and “a blue pizza” that appear elsewhere in the paper illustrate the rarity gradient across the dataset, not within-pair variation. Primary models for generation and denoiser-side intervention are SD1.5 and SDXL, while SD3 is used only for text-path diagnostic extension. For UNet block-group analysis, we partition cross-attention modules by their position in the UNet architecture. Following standard notation, D k D_{k} denotes the k k -th down-sampling (encoder) stage, M M the middle bottleneck, and U k U_{k} the k k -th up-sampling (decoder) stage. SDXL has five active cross-attention groups: { D 1 , D 2 , M , U 0 , U 1 } \{D_{1},D_{2},M,U_{0},U_{1}\} ; SD1.5 has seven: { D 0 , D 1 , D 2 , M , U 1 , U 2 , U 3 } \{D_{0},D_{1},D_{2},M,U_{1},U_{2},U_{3}\} (module counts per group in Appendix K ). Throughout, we refer to D 2 D_{2} as the deep encoder and U 0 U_{0} (SDXL) / U 1 U_{1} (SD1.5) as the decoder . With these sites defined, we next introduce two diagnostic readouts—one at the text encoder, one inside the denoiser—and two families of intervention: embedding-level repair and denoiser-side cross-attention edits. Text-encoder diagnostic: CSI. We operationalize text-side compositionality as a component-reconstruction test. If the text encoder preserves a factorized representation of attribute, object, and context, then a simple composition rule should explain the full-prompt embedding; large residuals indicate prompt-specific interactions beyond this factorized account. For each prompt p full p_{\mathrm{full}} (e.g., “a studio photo of a blue pizza”), we construct component inputs: p attr p_{\mathrm{attr}} (the target attribute, e.g., “blue”), p obj p_{\mathrm{obj}} (the object, e.g., “pizza”), and p ctx p_{\mathrm{ctx}} (the surrounding context template). Let h ⁡ ( ⋅ ) h(\cdot) denote the representation extracted from the text encoder, and let h ^ ​ ( ⋅ ) \hat{h}(\cdot) be a deliberately low-capacity composition model fit to predict h ⁡ ( p full ) h(p_{\mathrm{full}}) from the component representations. We consider additive, low-rank linear, and low-rank bilinear variants, fit on anchor prompts and evaluated on both anchor and stress prompts. We define the non-factorization residual as R ⁡ ( p full ) = ‖ h ⁡ ( p full ) − h ^ ​ ( p attr , p obj , p ctx ) ‖ 2 ‖ h ⁡ ( p full ) ‖ 2 + ε . R(p_{\mathrm{full}})=\frac{\left\lVert h(p_{\mathrm{full}})-\hat{h}(p_{\mathrm{attr}},p_{\mathrm{obj}},p_{\mathrm{ctx}})\right\rVert_{2}}{\left\lVert h(p_{\mathrm{full}})\right\rVert_{2}+\varepsilon}. (1) where ε \varepsilon prevents division by zero. In plain terms: If the encoder preserves component-wise structure for “blue,” “pizza,” and the context template, then a simple composition model should be able to reconstruct the full-prompt embedding, yielding a small R R . If the full prompt instead induces prompt-specific interactions that are not predictable from those components, the residual increases. CSI aggregates this normalized residual with span-geometry features via robust standardization on anchor statistics; we report CSI text \mathrm{CSI}_{\mathrm{text}} , CSI span \mathrm{CSI}_{\mathrm{span}} , and combined CSI \mathrm{CSI} . Only CSI text \mathrm{CSI}_{\mathrm{text}} is strictly pre-denoising; combined CSI includes internal attention-derived span features. For each UNet block group b b , diagnostic accessibility DA ⁡ ( b ) \mathrm{DA}(b) measures how well block-level cross-attention patterns distinguish anchor from stress prompts during baseline generation. To separate where an intervention is applied from what kind of intervention it is, we organize denoiser-side edits along two axes: selectivity , whether the edit targets only the attribute token or the entire cross-attention map, and sign , whether the edit strengthens or weakens the conditioning channel. This gives a 2 × 2 2{\times}2 design; the broad-additive cell is omitted because uniformly scaling all attention weights is canceled by post-softmax normalization, leaving three testable denoiser-side families. Selective additive ( boost ) amplifies attention to the target attribute token at a chosen block, testing whether stronger local attribute readout improves binding. Selective subtractive ( attr_zero ) removes the same attribute-token attention, testing the opposite direction as a matched-selectivity control. Broad subtractive ( zero ) uniformly flattens all cross-attention at a chosen block, testing whether the block’s entire text-conditioning contribution is necessary or harmful. Together with two embedding-level repair families—pooled and token low-rank adapters trained to move stress representations toward anchor-like structure—this yields five intervention families. Implementation details and statistical testing protocols are given in Appendix D . These three denoiser modalities span a natural hypothesis space about the defect’s structure. If the failure reflects weak attribute readout, boost should help by amplifying the target-attribute channel. If the same channel is causally involved but harmful or mislocalized, attr_zero tests the opposite direction by removing it. If the failure is distributed across the block’s entire text-conditioning pathway, zero tests whether removing that contribution improves generation. Testing all three at each block allows us to diagnose not just where the defect is, but what kind of defect it is. These findings support evaluating diagnostic readouts and intervention operators separately, with the strength of each comparison stated explicitly. 7 Discussion Taken together, the upstream and downstream analyses reveal a specific property of diffusion pipelines: as the conditioning representation flows from text encoder to denoiser cross-attention, the features that are most informative about which prompts will fail and the features that are most responsive to interventions that correct failure live in different places. Text-encoder residuals provide a diagnostic coordinate; D2 has the largest positive signed DA mean; and decoder blocks have the largest positive boost CE means. Together these measurements locate distinct diagnostic and intervention-response profiles along the pipeline. The site-level mismatch extends to the prompt level as well: CSI-stratified analysis shows no consistent positive correlation between pre-denoising stress severity and decoder boost response (SDXL partial ρ = − 0.17 \rho{=}-0.17 , p = 0.007 p{=}0.007 ; SD1.5 ρ = + 0.11 \rho{=}+0.11 , ns), so diagnostic severity does not predict which prompts respond to intervention. Diagnosis and intervention are not aligned by default along the pipeline; whether they can be realigned depends on choices about objective (embedding repair, § 5 ) and modality (per-block decomposition, § 6 ), not merely site. Two mechanistic observations sharpen the dissociation. At D2, neither tested token-level intervention shows an FDR-significant CHR effect and per-timestep analysis shows DA–CE anti-correlation—D2 is most diagnostic in early denoising precisely when boost is most destructive. We interpret this carefully: our tested attribute-token operators (additive boost, matched-selectivity zeroing, fractional attenuation) do not reach the defect, but the underlying structure is not uniquely identified, since the pattern is equally consistent with a distributed defect across D2’s cross-attention output and with a localized defect in a representation subspace our operators miss. At the decoder, U0’s negative DA ( − 0.0118 -0.0118 , FDR q = 0.00033 q{=}0.00033 in the SDXL boost baseline) indicates a reverse anchor–stress ABM contrast; the decoder does not lack signal but faithfully executes whatever binding it receives, including incorrect upstream binding. Overriding existing binding with a competing signal is one possible interpretation, not a mechanism established by these comparisons. These findings motivate evaluating diagnostic readouts and intervention operators jointly while selecting intervention sites using measured output responses. Beyond our own protocol, the modality–site dissociation has implications for existing inference-time methods. Attend-and-Excite [ 4 ] and SynGen [ 28 ] apply gradient-based corrections across all cross-attention layers simultaneously; our per-block decomposition suggests their effectiveness may concentrate at decoder blocks, because decoder blocks have the largest positive boost CE means in our sweeps. If the encoder-side contribution is zero or negative, all-layer methods may succeed despite their encoder-side component rather than because of it—a testable prediction: restricting A&E/SynGen updates to decoder-only cross-attention should preserve or improve performance while reducing compute, and restricting to encoder-only should degrade performance to baseline or worse. More broadly, the diagnosis–control mismatch is not specific to diffusion models. Any system with a separated encoder and decoder—including encoder-decoder language models, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, and vision-language models—faces the same structural question: does diagnosing a defect in the encoder tell you how to fix it in the decoder? Our results suggest the answer is not automatic. The features that make a defect visible (high mutual information with the anchor/stress label) need not be the features that make it fixable (responsive to targeted intervention). Intervention design must be informed by the decoder’s readout structure, not merely by the encoder’s diagnostic signal. 7.1 Scope and Interpretation The central conclusion of this work is not that a particular intervention site universally solves compositional failures. Rather, our evidence establishes that diagnostic accessibility, representation modification, and semantic improvement should not be assumed to coincide. Accordingly, we do not claim (i) that all upstream interventions fail, (ii) that decoder-side intervention provides a universal repair mechanism, or (iii) that the observed diagnosis-control dissociation has been established for relational or role-binding compositions. Our results are supported for the evaluated attribute-object setting and the tested intervention modalities. 8 Limitations We distinguish established from suggestive findings. Established : (i) CSI separates anchor from stress cross-model (ROC-AUC = 1.0 {=}1.0 , permutation null = 0.49 {=}0.49 , within-stress ρ = 0.68 \rho{=}0.68 ), though partly reflecting the controlled protocol; (ii) D2 has the largest positive signed DA mean in the six baseline datasets and differs from zero after FDR; these are not six independent replications; (iii) selective subtraction shows no significant positive CHR effect across the reported blocks; (iv) embedding repair reduces residuals without semantic improvement. Suggestive : (v) decoder boost as a preferred selective site (baseline contrasts nominally significant in both models but not after per-block FDR; decoder-minus-D2 significant only in SDXL); (vi) D2 defect structure (consistent with but not uniquely identified by our operators); (vii) generality beyond chromatic binding. Key caveats: boost CE is small ( + 0.006 +0.006 – 0.008 0.008 ) and does not survive within-model FDR; CE is color-only (52 valid prompts per seed); SD3 is text-path only; two UNet architectures, no DiT; fixed intervention hyperparameters; CSI-based routing and a universal decoder repair interface unvalidated; broad-additive cell untested; WiCLP-aligned embedding repair not tested; object mask from baseline attention, held fixed across conditions (empirically verified stable: median | Δ | = 0.2 % |\Delta|{=}0.2\% , p ​ 95 = 1.5 % p95{=}1.5\% , r ≥ 0.92 r{\geq}0.92 ). We characterize a modality-dependent structure, not a universal law. External-mask and background-color sensitivity checks further limit the interpretation to a small chromatic response rather than established object-local semantic repair (Appendix J ). 9 Conclusion We characterize compositional diagnosis and intervention through complementary measurements of text representations, cross-attention, and generated color agreement. Text-only CSI provides an upstream stress coordinate across SD1.5, SDXL, and the SD3 text path under the controlled anchor–stress protocol. Within the two tested UNets, the largest positive signed DA mean occurs at D2, while the largest positive selective-boost CE mean occurs at decoder blocks. A matched six-prompt localization study further links intervention location to output response, with downstream intervention increasing CHR as residual-minimizing adapters improve representation fit. Broad ablation reveals distinct architecture-dependent sensitivity profiles. Together, these findings provide an empirical site–modality map and motivate choosing intervention sites through output-response evaluation alongside diagnostic analysis. Extending this framework to broader compositional benchmarks, binding-aligned objectives, and DiT backbones offers concrete directions for future work.
